entry.evidence: Concurrently, δ18O was distinguishably lower (−0.55~−0.6‰) when compared to four years of available data

steps.action: Posed the open question of how oceanic surface heating and the resulting Shallow Mode meltwater affect the adjacent ocean, against the community view that this mode is negligible.
steps.quote: However, the processes of oceanic surface heating and impact of the resultant meltwater on the adjacent ocean has not been investigated yet.

steps.action: Set out a design that combines ship and mooring hydrography (including originally developed profilers), δ18O water sampling, satellite SST and sea-ice data, and an ocean–sea ice–ice shelf model.
steps.quote: the behavior of glacial meltwater fraction in seawater discerned using the stable oxygen isotope ratio (δ18O) obtained by ship-board and time-series water samplings

steps.action: Observed anomalously warm satellite SST in February 2017, upper-ocean CTD temperatures at CDP 0.5–1 °C warmer than in other years, and distinctly lower δ18O.
steps.quote: the temperature at 0–100 m depths was ~0.5–1 °C warmer in 2017 compared to the other [...]

steps.action: Inferred the glacial meltwater fraction with a three-endmember salinity–δ18O mixing model (Methods §3.2), giving 1.3–1.9% at 50 m in February 2017, 0.5 ± 0.1% above the other years.
steps.quote: The glacial meltwater fraction was 1.3% for the lower bound and 1.9% for the upper bound at 50 m depth in February 2017

steps.action: Bounded the meltwater-fraction estimate by varying the glacial δ18O endmember between the ice-core value (−40‰) and the iceberg value (−27‰), its largest source of uncertainty (Methods).
steps.quote: To derive lower- and upper- bounds of the glacial estimates, we use the observed estimates of ice cores of AIS (−40‰) and icebergs

steps.action: Checked the warm, meltwater-rich layer at an independent station on the shelf break off CDP and found the same 2017 signal.
steps.quote: which indicates that the higher meltwater content observation was robust and broadly distributed

steps.action: Documented from satellite SST and sea-ice concentration, and from ship photographs, that summer 2017 was warm and nearly ice-free at CDP, unlike 2018.
steps.quote: the 2017 summer was warm with high SST and low SIC

steps.action: Established from the 35-year satellite record that warm summers (2001, 2003, 2004, 2010, 2017) recur with low sea-ice concentration, as a significant negative SST–SIC correlation.
steps.quote: with a correlation coefficient of −0.82 (−0.77) for the PB (AIS) region over the 35 years from 1986–2020

steps.action: Explained the SST–SIC covariation with the published open water/ice-albedo feedback.
steps.quote: [...] be explained by the open water/ice-albedo feedback

steps.action: Observed in ice-front profiles (ship, WOD and MEOP seal data) a thick warm AASW layer in February 2017 extending below the 250 m ice draft, deeper than in other years.
steps.quote: Temperature profiles in February 2017 revealed a thick layer of warmer AASW, extending well below the ice shelf draft depth of 250 m

steps.action: Screened the MEOP biologging profiles by visual inspection and by comparison with representative ship-based profiles before use (Methods).
steps.quote: only the most realistic files were used after visual inspection and broad comparison with representative ship-based profiles

steps.action: Hypothesized that easterly-wind Ekman convergence deepens warm AASW below the ice-front draft, so that it subducts into the cavity and drives basal melt.
steps.quote: it can subduct into the cavity beneath the ice shelf and supply heat for the basal melt

steps.action: Checked that the ocean–sea ice–ice shelf hindcast reproduces the warm 2017 summer and the timing of interannual SST and SIC variability (Supplementary Fig. 5; Methods §3.4 ¶3).
steps.quote: Our numerical simulation replicates the features of the warm 2017 summer in PB

steps.action: Computed modeled basal melt from the 1979–2018 hindcast (configuration after ref. 44, three-equation melt): highest front melt in 2017 (>6 m per month) and 22.6 Gt summer melt, 12.7 Gt above the climatology.
steps.quote: the model produces higher basal melt at the front of the AIS in 2017 and in other warm summers

steps.action: Compared the spatial pattern of simulated melt with the observed distribution of high SST and warm AASW at depth.
steps.quote: consistent with the distribution of high SST and warm AASW at depth

steps.action: Recorded over-winter mooring time series at CDP in 2017 (δ18O sampler, profiler, current meter), showing that the high meltwater fraction persisted into June.
steps.quote: revealed the high values observed in summer continued to early winter around June

steps.action: Estimated an advection distance of about 450 km from the mean current speed and an observed excess meltwater volume of about 13.5 Gt from the 0.5% anomaly and an assumed volume flux.
steps.quote: The volume of melt water is estimated to be about 13.5 Gt

steps.action: Compared the observation-based 13.5 Gt with the modeled 12.7 Gt summer melt anomaly, which supports an AIS origin for the CDP meltwater.
steps.quote: The consistency of this estimation with the modeled summer melt anomaly at the AIS terminus (12.7 Gt) supports the idea

steps.action: Compared the basal meltwater volume with published in situ, satellite and model estimates for the AIS (27–52 Gt per year).
steps.quote: The volume of basal meltwater obtained in this study is comparable to previous estimates.

steps.action: Excluded surface meltwater runoff as the source, because the published 2016/17 runoff peak (<1 Gt) is an order of magnitude smaller than basal melt.
steps.quote: Hence the volume of glacial meltwater discharged into the nearby ocean is dominated by the basal melting of AIS/PIS.

steps.action: Hypothesized that warm AASW and meltwater input delay dense shelf water formation, by delaying sea-ice growth and altering the winter mixed layer.
steps.quote: can impact the formation of DSW in the subsequent autumn/winter by determining the onset of sustained sea-ice growth

steps.action: Compared the 2017 and 2019 mooring temperature records and found that near-surface cooling, and cooling to freezing at 164 m, came a week to a few weeks later in 2017 (Figure 4, p. 5).
steps.quote: time series of ocean temperature profiles in autumn 2017 revealed about a week delay in near-surface cooling compared with autumn 2019

steps.action: Checked the delayed freeze-up against independent satellite-derived sea-ice production, across the five warm years and the three Prydz Bay polynyas.
steps.quote: Independent observational evidence concurs that the initiation of sea-ice production was impacted by the warmer AASW in 2017.

steps.action: Compared the timing of salinity reaching the 34.5 DSW criterion and found it about three weeks later in 2017 than in 2019 (Figure 4, p. 5).
steps.quote: the observed increase in salinity from autumn to early-winter was slower in 2017 by about three weeks

steps.action: Excluded weaker sea-ice production as the cause of the slow salinification, since 2019 had even less initial production, and attributed it to advected AIS meltwater.
steps.quote: Hence the slower salinity increase in 2017 must result from other sources of freshwater, very likely due to the glacial meltwater advected from the AIS.

steps.action: Kept the claim that summer AASW heat storage triggers extra AIS melt whose advected freshening delays DSW emergence at CDP by about three weeks.
steps.quote: causes a delay of about three weeks in the emergence of DSW in the CDP

steps.action: Placed 2017 in context with the published record-low 2016 spring circumpolar sea-ice extent and the widespread warm AASW.
steps.quote: the sea-ice extent in the preceding spring was the minimum across the 40-year record on the circumpolar scale

steps.action: Used published projections of future Southern Ocean sea-ice loss to argue that 2017 conditions could become the new normal.
steps.quote: Future predictions of the Southern Ocean indicate a broad loss of sea-ice cover in association with global warming

steps.action: Refined the view of ice-shelf melt regimes: Shallow Mode melting will gain importance for bottom water formation and sea level projections.
steps.quote: there will be an step-increase in the importance and impact of Shallow Mode ice shelf melting

end.claim: Excess summer heat storage in Antarctic Surface Water in Prydz Bay triggered additional basal meltwater from the Amery Ice Shelf, whose advection to Cape Darnley delayed the emergence of dense shelf water by about three weeks in 2017.

decisive_move.sentence: The δ18O three-endmember estimate of an anomalous glacial meltwater fraction (0.5 ± 0.1% above other years), carried through the mooring time series, is what links warm AASW to extra ice-shelf melt and to the slowed salinification; without it only the heat effect would remain.

gates.evidence: The hydrography and moorings are routine JARE observations at CDP, deployed before the warm-summer meltwater hypothesis is stated (inference: the 2017 mooring was not placed to test it). The claim faced checks it could have failed: the observation-based meltwater volume (13.5 Gt) had to match the modeled anomaly (12.7 Gt), and the sea-ice production contrast with 2019 could have explained the salinity lag. Both are post hoc and qualitative. Nothing is reported as fixed before the data; the 15 km3 SIP criterion and the 34.5 DSW criterion (from ref. 18) are chosen without stated pre-specification.

limits: Only the published text was coded. A peer review file is listed (§A1.1 ¶1) but was not supplied, so no review sequence exists. Sub-claims at other statuses: the summer SST–SIC anticorrelation is regularity_in_range (1986–2020, r = −0.82/−0.77); the meltwater fraction anomaly is estimate_with_resolution (0.5 ± 0.1%, bounded by endmembers); the modeled melt volumes (22.6, 12.7, 69.2 Gt) are estimates given without uncertainty; the attribution of meltwater to AIS basal melt is best_explanation ("hypothesised"); the future Shallow Mode increase is an untested projection. The direct meltwater evidence rests on one δ18O station per year and four years of data, and the DSW delay on a single 2017 versus 2019 mooring comparison. 2019 is not shown to be a normal year beyond its sea-ice production. Internal inconsistencies the text leaves unresolved: mooring meltwater depth 176 m (§2.2 ¶4) versus a sampler at 150 m (§3.1 ¶2); the hindcast spans 1979–2018 yet a 40-year period and a 1979–2019 climatology are cited; the DSW duration loss is printed as "~0%" (§2.3 ¶4). The model is not run with alternative forcings or without the 2017 anomaly, so the causal chain from heat to melt is not isolated (inference). No pre-registration or blinding is reported.
